response.content:
# Technical Brief: Optimizing Compiler Internals

This brief surveys eight core areas of optimizing compiler construction. For each area, at least three specific, named mechanisms are treated in depth, with attention to the invariants they maintain, their asymptotic behavior, and their interaction with the rest of the compilation pipeline.

---

## 1. SSA Construction

Static Single Assignment form requires that every variable have exactly one static definition point, with merge points of control flow reconciled via φ-functions. The central engineering problem is placing φ-functions minimally and renaming uses correctly.

### 1.1 Cytron et al.'s Dominance-Frontier Algorithm (Minimal SSA)

The classical algorithm (Cytron, Ferrante, Rosen, Wegman, Zadeck, 1991) places φ-functions using **dominance frontiers**. The dominance frontier DF(X) of a block X is the set of blocks Y such that X dominates a predecessor of Y but does not strictly dominate Y itself — i.e., the "first" blocks where X's dominance ceases. For each variable v, a φ-function is needed at the **iterated dominance frontier** DF⁺(Defs(v)): the least fixed point of applying DF to the set of definition blocks, because φ-functions are themselves definitions and may induce further φ placement. After placement, a **renaming pass** walks the dominator tree with a per-variable version stack: at each definition a fresh version is pushed; at each use the top of stack is read; at each successor block's φ-functions, the operand corresponding to the current edge is filled in; stacks are popped on exit from the dominator-tree node. This yields **minimal SSA** (φ only where two distinct definitions genuinely meet). Combined with liveness information it yields **pruned SSA** (no φ for dead variables); a cheaper compromise is **semi-pruned SSA** (Briggs), which places φ only for variables live across block boundaries ("non-locals"), avoiding full liveness computation.

### 1.2 Lengauer–Tarjan Dominator Computation (and Cooper–Harvey–Kennedy)

Dominance-frontier-based construction presupposes the **dominator tree**. The **Lengauer–Tarjan algorithm** (1979) computes immediate dominators in near-linear time, O(E α(E,V)) with path compression, using the notion of **semidominators**: sdom(w) is the minimum-DFS-number vertex from which w is reachable via a path whose intermediate nodes all have higher DFS numbers than w. A two-phase pass over the DFS tree converts semidominators into immediate dominators via link-eval forest operations. In practice, many production compilers (LLVM historically, and others) use the **Cooper–Harvey–Kennedy iterative algorithm** ("A Simple, Fast Dominance Algorithm"), a worklist fixpoint over `idom` approximations in reverse post-order with a clever two-finger `intersect` routine that walks up the partially built dominator tree. Despite worse asymptotic bounds (O(V²) worst case), its small constants and cache-friendly data layout make it faster on real CFGs. LLVM later moved to a **semi-NCA** (semidominator + nearest-common-ancestor) hybrid, which also supports incremental dominator-tree updates needed by transformation passes.

### 1.3 Braun et al.'s On-the-Fly SSA Construction

Braun, Buchwald, Hack, Leißa, Mallon, Zwinkau (CC 2013) construct SSA **directly from the AST/bytecode without a prior CFG analysis**, as used in Cranelift, libFirm, and Go's frontend lowering. The algorithm maintains, per basic block, a map from source variables to current SSA values. `readVariable(v, B)` in a **sealed** block (all predecessors known) with multiple predecessors recursively reads from predecessors and inserts a φ; in an **unsealed** block (e.g., a loop header still being built), it inserts an **operandless φ** recorded as incomplete, whose operands are filled in when the block is sealed. Crucially, trivial φ-functions — those whose operands are all the same value or the φ itself — are removed via `tryRemoveTrivialPhi`, which recursively re-examines users, yielding minimal SSA on reducible CFGs **without ever computing dominance frontiers**. The paper also shows that with on-the-fly removal of redundant φ-cycles (via SCC detection, à la Tarjan), minimality holds on irreducible graphs too. This is attractive for JITs because it fuses parsing, CFG construction, and SSA renaming into one pass.

### 1.4 SSA Destruction (out-of-SSA)

Leaving SSA is nontrivial: naïvely converting each φ into copies in predecessor blocks breaks in the presence of **critical edges** and produces the **lost-copy** and **swap problems** (φ-congruence cycles requiring a temporary). **Sreedhar et al.'s method** eliminates φ-interference by placing copies to establish **φ-congruence classes** whose members never interfere; **Boissinot et al. (CGO 2009)** give a correctness-first revision using liveness and value-equivalence checks, parallel-copy sequentialization, and dominance-based interference tests. Modern allocators (e.g., SSA-based register allocation, §3) may instead keep SSA until after allocation and materialize parallel copies during coloring.

---

## 2. Alias Analysis

Alias analysis (pointer analysis) determines whether two memory references may, must, or cannot refer to the same location. Precision axes: **flow-sensitivity**, **context-sensitivity**, **field-sensitivity**, and **inclusion vs. unification** constraint solving.

### 2.1 Andersen's Inclusion-Based Analysis

Andersen's analysis (1994) is **flow-insensitive, inclusion-based**: each pointer variable p has a points-to set pts(p), and assignments generate **subset constraints** — `p = &x` yields x ∈ pts(p); `p = q` yields pts(q) ⊆ pts(p); `p = *q` yields ∀v ∈ pts(q): pts(v) ⊆ pts(p); `*p = q` yields ∀v ∈ pts(p): pts(q) ⊆ pts(v). Solving is a dynamic transitive closure over a constraint graph, worst-case **O(n³)** ("cubic bottleneck"). Scalability comes from **online cycle elimination** (nodes in a cycle of inclusion edges provably have equal points-to sets and are collapsed — Fähndrich et al.; "Lazy Cycle Detection" and "Hybrid Cycle Detection" of Hardekopf & Lin, PLDI 2007), **wave/deep propagation** ordering, and **BDD- or bitmap-based** points-to set representations. Andersen's is the precision baseline for flow-insensitive analysis and underlies GCC's `-fipa-pta` and many whole-program frameworks (e.g., SVF for LLVM).

### 2.2 Steensgaard's Unification-Based Analysis

Steensgaard (POPL 1996) trades precision for speed: assignments induce **equality constraints** rather than subset constraints — `p = q` **unifies** the abstract locations pointed to by p and q using a **union-find** structure. The result is an **almost-linear O(n α(n))** analysis producing a storage-shape graph where each node has at most one points-to successor. Precision loss is substantial (unification is symmetric: assigning q into p also pollutes q), but the near-linear cost makes it the choice for enormous codebases, link-time passes under tight budgets, and as a fast pre-pass to partition the problem for a more precise analysis. One-level-flow variants (Das, PLDI 2000) recover much of Andersen's precision at near-Steensgaard cost by using inclusion at the top pointer level and unification below.

### 2.3 Type-Based Alias Analysis (TBAA)

TBAA exploits language-level typing rules — in C/C++, the **strict aliasing rule** (C11 §6.5p7): an object may only be accessed through an lvalue of a compatible type, a signed/unsigned/qualified variant, or a character type. The compiler builds a **type DAG / aliasing hierarchy**; two accesses whose effective types are unrelated in this hierarchy are declared NoAlias without any pointer tracking. LLVM encodes this as `!tbaa` metadata on loads/stores, with **struct-path TBAA** refining precision to distinguish distinct fields of the same aggregate (access paths like `struct S → field f at offset k`). Diebold & classic reference: Diwan, McKinley, Moss (PLDI 1998) for Modula-3. TBAA is cheap and powerful for scheduling and vectorization but is **unsound in the presence of type punning**, hence `-fno-strict-aliasing` escape hatches and careful interaction with `memcpy`-based reinterpretation and `union` rules.

### 2.4 Shape and Context-Sensitive Refinements

Beyond the big three: **k-CFA / k-object-sensitive** analyses add calling-context or allocation-site-receiver context to points-to sets (Milanova's object sensitivity dominates call-string sensitivity for OO languages); **Data Structure Analysis (DSA)** (Lattner & Adve) is a unification-based, context-sensitive, field-sensitive heap analysis producing per-function points-to graphs with heap cloning; **Basic Alias Analysis** in LLVM (`BasicAA`) is a stateless, intraprocedural, rule-based decision procedure (distinct identified objects don't alias; GEP offset arithmetic; `noalias`/`restrict` attributes implementing C99 `restrict` semantics; escape-based arguments). Production compilers stack these as a **chain of responders**: BasicAA → TBAA → scoped-noalias → globals AA, returning the first definitive answer.

---

## 3. Register Allocation

The problem: map an unbounded set of virtual registers/live ranges onto k physical registers, inserting **spill** code (store/reload), **splits**, and **copies** while minimizing dynamic cost. NP-hard in general (reduction from graph coloring), but SSA-form interference graphs are **chordal**, making optimal coloring polynomial (spilling remains hard).

### 3.1 Chaitin–Briggs Graph Coloring

Chaitin (1981/82) models allocation as coloring the **interference graph**: nodes are live ranges; edges connect ranges simultaneously live. The algorithm iterates: **build** (interference graph from liveness), **coalesce** (merge copy-related non-interfering nodes), **simplify** (repeatedly remove nodes of degree < k onto a stack — Kempe's reduction: such a node is trivially colorable), **spill decision** when no low-degree node remains, **select** (pop and assign colors). Chaitin spills eagerly ("spill everywhere"); **Briggs's optimistic coloring** (1994) instead pushes a high-degree node onto the stack anyway, deferring the spill decision to select time — the node may still color if its neighbors share colors. Briggs also introduced **conservative coalescing** (coalesce only if the merged node has < k neighbors of significant degree, guaranteeing no new spills), later refined by **George–Appel iterated register coalescing (IRC)**, which interleaves simplify/coalesce/freeze phases with worklists so copies are coalesced aggressively but safely. Spill cost heuristics weigh use/def frequency (scaled by loop depth, typically 10^depth) against degree. Rematerialization (Briggs/Cooper): instead of spilling, recompute never-killed values (constants, address computations) at use points.

### 3.2 Linear Scan and Second-Chance Binpacking

**Linear scan** (Poletto & Sarkar, 1999) sacrifices precision for near-linear compile time, historically dominant in JITs (HotSpot client compiler, early V8, LLVM's old `-regalloc=linearscan`). Live ranges are approximated as **intervals** over a linearized instruction order; a single sweep maintains an **active list**, expiring intervals whose endpoints have passed and spilling (typically the interval with the **furthest end point** — a Belady-flavored heuristic) when registers are exhausted. **Wimmer–Mössenböck's linear scan with interval splitting** (HotSpot) handles **lifetime holes** (ranges where a value is live but with gaps) and splits intervals at arbitrary positions, inserting moves, plus **use-position weights** to choose split points outside loops. **Traub's second-chance binpacking** allows a spilled interval to re-enter a register later. SSA-based linear scan (Wimmer & Franz, CGO 2010) exploits the property that SSA liveness intervals, ordered by dominance, allow allocation without an explicit interference graph.

### 3.3 Priority-Based / Live-Range-Splitting Allocators (LLVM Greedy)

LLVM's **Greedy Register Allocator** (Olesen, 2011) assigns live ranges in **priority order** (weighted by spill cost and size — descendants of Chow–Hennessy's **priority-based coloring**, 1984/1990, which allocated in priority order with live-range splitting as the fallback instead of spilling). Ranges are enqueued; on allocation failure the allocator attempts, in order: **eviction** (displace an already-assigned cheaper range), **live-range splitting** guided by the CFG (region splitting around loop boundaries using an edge-bundle/Hopfield-network model to place split points where moves are cheapest), **last-chance local splitting**, and finally **spilling** with an inline spiller that performs **spill-slot coalescing** and rematerialization. This architecture decouples the global decision (which range gets a register in which region) from the local one and generally beats both pure Chaitin–Briggs and linear scan on performance of generated code.

### 3.4 PBQP and SSA-Based Allocation (brief)

Two further named mechanisms worth knowing: **PBQP allocation** (Scholz & Eckstein) encodes allocation as a Partitioned Boolean Quadratic Problem — cost vectors per virtual register (per physical-register and spill options) and cost matrices per interference/coalescing pair — solved by dynamic-programming reductions (R0/R1/R2) with heuristics for irreducible nodes; it elegantly handles irregular architectures (paired registers, register aliases such as x86 AH/AL, ARM LDRD constraints). **SSA-based register allocation** (Hack, Grund, Goos) colors the chordal interference graph of a program *still in SSA form* optimally in O(n·k) via a perfect elimination order given by the dominator tree, pushing all NP-hardness into the spilling and copy-coalescing phases, with φ-destruction realized as parallel copies after assignment.

---

## 4. Inlining

Inlining (procedure integration) replaces a call with the callee's body. It is the single most important enabler of other optimizations (it manufactures context) but inflates code size and compile time; the core problem is the **cost/benefit decision**, which is NP-hard under a global size budget (knapsack-like).

### 4.1 Bottom-Up Inlining over the SCC Call Graph with Cost Models (LLVM)

LLVM's inliner walks the **call graph in bottom-up order over strongly connected components** (callees before callers; SCCs handle mutual recursion), so that a callee is itself fully simplified before its size/benefit is measured, and so that inlining decisions compose (the "inline, then simplify, then reconsider callers" loop — the pass manager re-runs function simplification on the merged body and revisits new call sites). The decision is a **threshold model**: `InlineCost` sums per-instruction costs over the callee under a symbolic simulation that accounts for **call-site-specific simplification** — constant arguments propagate, branches on them fold and remove whole blocks from the cost, allocas passed as pointers get SROA bonuses — compared against a threshold adjusted by hints (`inlinehint`, `alwaysinline`, `noinline`), optimization level (`-Oz` shrinks thresholds), callee attributes (`cold` callsites get slashed thresholds), and a **vector/branch-fold bonus**. Key named ingredients: the **cost-benefit analysis with cycle savings vs. size growth** gated by profile data when available, and **deferred inlining** (inlining a call might be better done after the caller itself is inlined upward). GCC's `ipa-inline` is structurally similar with `--param inline-unit-growth` global budgets and **fibonacci-heap-ordered greedy inlining by badness** (benefit/size ratio), an explicit **greedy knapsack approximation**.

### 4.2 Profile-Guided and Priority-Driven Inlining

With **PGO** (instrumentation-based or sampling-based, e.g., AutoFDO/SamplePGO), edge/call-site frequencies replace static heuristics: hot call sites get raised thresholds, cold ones get suppressed (controlling **i-cache pressure**, the dominant cost of over-inlining on large servers). LLVM's **ML-guided inlining (MLGO)** replaces the hand-tuned heuristic with a trained policy for the -Oz size decision. The **top-down, priority-based inliner in the SamplePGO pipeline** performs inlining *before* profile annotation matching so the context-sensitive profile (e.g., **CSSPGO** with pseudo-instrumentation) can attribute counts to inlined instances. The essential named concept: **context-sensitive profiles** make the benefit side of the cost model accurate per call site rather than per callee.

### 4.3 Speculative Inlining and Devirtualization (JIT-Style)

In JVMs and JS engines, most interesting calls are virtual/dynamic. **Class Hierarchy Analysis (CHA)** (Dean, Grove, Chambers) proves monomorphism when only one loaded class implements a method, permitting direct inlining **guarded by a deoptimization dependency**: if class loading later invalidates the assumption, compiled code is discarded (**deoptimization / on-stack replacement** machinery, HotSpot). Where CHA fails, **inline caches** and **type-feedback–based receiver profiling** support **guarded inlining**: emit a class check (or method-pointer check) and inline the hot target, falling back to a virtual dispatch or an **uncommon trap** on the slow path; **polymorphic inline cache (PIC)**-derived profiles allow inlining 2–3 hot receivers (bimorphic/polymorphic inlining in HotSpot C2, Graal's **trivial/priority inlining** with explored call-tree expansion). This mechanism — speculate, guard, deoptimize — is the defining difference between JIT and AOT inlining.

### 4.4 Partial Inlining and Outlining (brief)

**Partial inlining** inlines only the hot prologue of a callee (e.g., the early-return fast path) and leaves the cold remainder as an **outlined** residual function called conditionally; LLVM's `partial-inliner` and **hot/cold splitting** cooperate with it. This addresses the common "guard-then-work" callee shape without paying full body duplication.

---

## 5. Escape Analysis

Escape analysis determines whether an object's lifetime or visibility escapes its allocating method/thread, enabling **stack allocation**, **scalar replacement**, **synchronization elision**, and allocation sinking.

### 5.1 Connection Graph Analysis (Choi et al.)

Choi, Gupta, Serrano, Sreedhar, Midkiff (OOPSLA 1999) — the canonical Java formulation. Build a **connection graph** per method: nodes for objects, references, and fields; edges for points-to, deferred (copy), and field relations. Escape states form a lattice: **NoEscape ⊏ ArgEscape ⊏ GlobalEscape**; states propagate over the graph (assignment to a static field, being thrown, or stored into an escaping object ⇒ GlobalEscape; passed to a callee ⇒ at least ArgEscape, refinable interprocedurally by mapping callee connection-graph summaries back through actual arguments). The analysis is flow-sensitive intraprocedurally with interprocedural **summary application** at call sites. Results: NoEscape objects become **stack-allocated or scalar-replaced**; non-thread-escaping objects allow **lock elision** (removing `monitorenter/monitorexit` on provably thread-local objects).

### 5.2 Partial Escape Analysis with Scalar Replacement (Graal)

Stadler, Würthinger, Mössenböck (CGO 2014): instead of a binary whole-method verdict, perform **flow-sensitive virtualization**: an allocation is kept **virtual** (represented as a compile-time map field→value, a "virtual object") as long as it hasn't escaped *along the current path*; at the first escaping use on some branch (store to heap, call, deopt point), the object is **materialized** only on that branch. Objects that never escape on hot paths are fully **scalar-replaced** (fields become SSA values; the allocation disappears), while cold escape paths pay a materialization. Deoptimization points receive **virtual-object descriptors** so the interpreter state can reconstruct the object lazily on deopt. This is strictly stronger than classic EA in branchy code and is the production design in GraalVM; HotSpot C2's EA (based on Choi et al. + reduction via **scalar replacement of aggregates** after macro expansion) is whole-method and correspondingly weaker on partially escaping objects.

### 5.3 Go's Escape Analysis (Address-Taken Flow Analysis for Stack Allocation)

Go's compiler (cmd/compile) decides stack vs. heap per allocation site with a **data-flow analysis over an assignment/flow graph with address-of and dereference weights**: each edge carries a derefs count (−1 for `&x`, +1 for `*p`); a value escapes if it flows, at non-negative cumulative deref level, to a sink with longer lifetime (return values, heap pointers, globals, closures capturing by reference, variadic `interface{}` boxes, channels). It is **interprocedural via per-function parameter summaries** ("escape tags" recorded in export data: does param leak to heap / to result k / not at all). Results dictate `new(T)`/composite literals staying on the stack, and interact with **inlining** (inlining removes call-boundary conservatism, a major reason Go inlining improves allocation behavior). Diagnosable via `-gcflags=-m`. The named mechanism to cite: **lifetime/leak summaries over a weighted flow graph**, in the lineage of the deref-counting formulation. Related compile-time mechanism in LLVM: **capture tracking / `nocapture` (now `captures(none)`) inference**, a lightweight escape analysis used by AA and by heap-to-stack promotion (`HeapToStack` in the Attributor), which converts `malloc`/`free` pairs of provably non-escaping, bounded-size objects into `alloca`s.

---

## 6. Loop Vectorization

Automatic conversion of scalar loops into SIMD form. Legality hinges on **data-dependence analysis** (loop-carried flow/anti/output dependences, distance/direction vectors); profitability on a cost model over the target's vector ISA.

### 6.1 Classic Loop Vectorization with Dependence Testing and If-Conversion

The Allen–Kennedy tradition: compute dependence using the **GCD test**, **Banerjee inequalities**, and exact tests (**Omega test**, Pugh — Presburger arithmetic via an extended Fourier–Motzkin elimination) on affine subscripts; a loop vectorizes by **VF** (vectorization factor) lanes if no loop-carried dependence has distance < VF (or dependences are of recognized idiom classes). Supporting transforms: **if-conversion** (replace control flow in the loop body with predicated/masked operations so the body becomes a single straight-line block — essential precondition for vectorizing conditional code, realized with vector masks/`select` or with full predication on SVE/AVX-512), **scalar expansion** and **reduction recognition** (sum/min/max/logical recurrences restructured into lane-parallel partial reductions plus a horizontal combine, exploiting reassociation permission from `-ffast-math` for FP), **recognition of first-order recurrences** and **induction variable** vectorization (step·⟨0,1,…,VF−1⟩ splats). LLVM's **LoopVectorize** implements this with **runtime alias checks** (emit overlap tests between pointer groups and branch to a scalar fallback loop — "memcheck" versioning), **tail folding by masking** vs. **scalar epilogue** loops, **interleaved access groups** (strided loads/stores turned into wide loads + shuffles), and an explicit **VPlan** infrastructure that models candidate vectorization strategies (VF × UF unroll-and-jam of the vector body, i.e., **interleaving**) and costs them before committing.

### 6.2 SLP Vectorization (Superword-Level Parallelism)

Larsen & Amarasinghe (PLDI 2000): instead of vectorizing across loop iterations, pack **isomorphic independent scalar instructions within straight-line code** into vector lanes. The algorithm seeds from **adjacent memory accesses** (consecutive loads/stores), builds packs, and extends them **bottom-up through use–def chains** (if `a0,a1` are packed and `ai = bi + ci`, try packing `b0,b1` and `c0,c1`), costing the saved scalar ops against inserted `insertelement/extractelement/shuffle` overhead ("gather" costs at tree leaves). LLVM's **SLPVectorizer** builds a **vectorizable tree** with scheduling-window legality checks; it complements the loop vectorizer (which often creates SLP opportunities after unrolling) and handles manually unrolled kernels, complex-number arithmetic, and RGBA-style struct code that loop vectorizers miss. Variants: **look-ahead SLP** operand reordering, **revectorization**, and **VectorCombine** cleanups.

### 6.3 Polyhedral Vectorization / Outer-Loop Strategies (brief but named)

The **polyhedral model** (see §8) enables vectorization beyond innermost loops: after computing exact dependence polyhedra, a scheduler (e.g., the **Pluto algorithm**) exposes a parallel innermost dimension via **loop interchange/skewing**, and codegen emits strip-mined (**strip-mining** = splitting an iteration space into chunks of VF) vector loops; **outer-loop vectorization** vectorizes an outer parallel loop while keeping inner loops scalar per lane (important for stencils; supported in LLVM via VPlan-native path, and in GCC's tree-vectorizer). Also name **scalable vectorization**: ARM **SVE/SVE2** and **RISC-V RVV** make VF a runtime quantity (`vscale` in LLVM IR), with **predication-based tail folding** (whole-loop predication via `get.active.lane.mask`) replacing epilogues entirely.

### 6.4 Gather/Scatter and Versioning Mechanics

Non-unit-stride and indirect accesses (`a[b[i]]`) vectorize via hardware **gather/scatter** instructions where profitable; **loop versioning** (runtime checks for aliasing, alignment, stride==1, trip count ≥ VF·UF) multi-versions the loop; **alignment peeling** runs scalar iterations until a pointer is aligned for aligned vector moves.

---

## 7. Instruction Scheduling

Reordering instructions to hide latency and maximize issue-width utilization, subject to data/control dependences and resource constraints. NP-hard even for basic blocks with latencies on realistic machines.

### 7.1 List Scheduling with Critical-Path Priority

The workhorse local scheduler: build the **data dependence DAG** of a basic block (edges labeled with latencies; include memory edges from alias analysis — this is where §2 pays off); maintain a **ready list** of instructions whose predecessors are scheduled and whose operands will be available; each cycle, pick ready instructions by a **priority function** — canonically **critical-path length** (maximum latency-weighted height to a DAG sink), tie-broken by successor count, register pressure impact, or source order — and issue them subject to a **resource/reservation-table model** of functional units and issue slots. Greedy list scheduling is a 2-approximation under standard assumptions (Graham bounds); quality hinges on the priority heuristic and the machine model. Production embodiments: LLVM's **MachineScheduler (MISched)** — a bidirectional (top-down + bottom-up) list scheduler over scheduling regions with a `GenericScheduler` policy balancing **register pressure sets** against latency (pressure tracking is first-class because pre-RA scheduling and allocation conflict), driven by per-subtarget **scheduling models** (per-opcode latencies, µop counts, processor resource usage, e.g., `SchedMachineModel` tables); GCC's Haifa scheduler is the analogous pre/post-RA list scheduler.

### 7.2 Trace Scheduling and Superblock Scheduling (Global Scheduling)

Basic blocks are too small (5–10 instructions) to fill wide machines. **Trace scheduling** (Fisher, 1981; the Multiflow compiler) selects a likely acyclic path (**trace**) through the CFG using profile estimates, schedules it as one long block, and inserts **bookkeeping/compensation code** on off-trace entries and exits to preserve semantics for instructions moved above side entrances or below side exits. The complexity of compensation at **join points** motivated **superblock scheduling** (Hwu et al., IMPACT): a superblock is a trace with **no side entrances**, formed by **tail duplication** (clone the blocks after each side entrance), so code may move upward freely past branches with simpler bookkeeping; combined with **superblock enlarging optimizations** (branch target expansion, loop peeling/unrolling). The hyperblock (Mahlke) extends this with **if-conversion/predication** to include multiple paths in one scheduling region on predicated ISAs (IA-64 lineage). These techniques are the backbone of VLIW compilation and survive in modern compilers as profile-guided block layout + bounded global code motion (e.g., LLVM's MachineSink / early if-conversion as weaker relatives).

### 7.3 Software Pipelining via Iterative Modulo Scheduling

For loops, overlap iterations: **software pipelining** seeks a schedule where iteration i+1 starts before i finishes, at a constant **initiation interval (II)**. **Iterative Modulo Scheduling** (Rau, MICRO 1994): compute lower bounds **ResMII** (resource-constrained minimum II: ceil of total unit demand / unit availability per resource) and **RecMII** (recurrence-constrained: for each dependence cycle C, ⌈latency(C)/distance(C)⌉, over elementary circuits of the loop DDG); try II = max(ResMII, RecMII), schedule operations into a **modulo reservation table** (resource usage conflicts are checked modulo II), using height-based priority with **backtracking/ejection** of conflicting ops; on failure, increment II and retry. The result is a kernel plus **prologue/epilogue**; overlapping lifetimes longer than II require **modulo variable expansion** (kernel unrolling with register renaming) or **rotating register files** (Itanium's hardware support, plus `br.ctop`-style special branches). Modern presence: LLVM's **MachinePipeliner** implements **swing modulo scheduling (SMS)** (Llosa et al.) — a non-backtracking variant ordering nodes to minimize register lifetime — targeting Hexagon and PowerPC.

### 7.4 Post-RA Scheduling and Hazard-Specific Mechanisms (brief)

After register allocation, **post-RA list scheduling** re-schedules around allocator-inserted spills with anti/output dependences now concrete; **hazard recognizers** model non-pipelined units, delay slots (classic MIPS **delayed-branch filling**), and in-order stall rules. Modern x86 backends mostly skip heavy post-RA scheduling (out-of-order cores) but still run **MacroFusion**-aware ordering (keep `cmp+jcc` adjacent) and mitigation-related scheduling constraints.

---

## 8. Loop Optimizations

High-level restructuring of loop nests for locality, parallelism, and reduced dynamic instruction count. (Vectorization, §6, is excluded here.)

### 8.1 Loop-Invariant Code Motion (LICM) and Scalar Promotion

Hoist computations whose operands are invariant in the loop into a **preheader** (a dedicated single-entry predecessor block; its existence is guaranteed by **loop simplification/canonicalization**: preheader insertion, single backedge via latch, dedicated exits — LoopSimplify in LLVM). Legality for hoisting a load requires dependence/alias reasoning: the location must not be modified in the loop (`MemorySSA` or AST — Alias Set Tracker — queries) and the hoist must not introduce faults on paths that didn't execute it (**speculation safety**: `isSafeToSpeculativelyExecute`, or guard with loop-guard dominance); sinking moves computations used only outside the loop into exits. **Scalar promotion (register promotion)** is LICM's memory form: if a memory location is loop-invariantly addressed, non-aliased, and dereferenceability/thread-safety conditions hold (beware data races: promotion of a conditional store to unconditional is illegal under C11 memory model unless the location is provably thread-local or already unconditionally accessed), replace loads/stores with a register carried by a φ and a single store in the exit. A stronger relative: **Lazy Code Motion (Knoop–Rüthing–Steffen)**, the optimal **partial redundancy elimination (PRE)** framework placing computations computationally optimal and lifetime-optimal via four dataflow problems (down-safety/up-safety i.e. anticipability/availability, earliest/latest); LICM is subsumed by PRE conceptually, and GVN-PRE (Thomas VanDrunen) merges it with value numbering.

### 8.2 Induction Variable Transformations: Strength Reduction, IV Canonicalization, and SCEV

**Operator strength reduction** replaces `i*c` inside a loop with an **auxiliary induction variable** incremented by c per iteration (Allen–Cocke–Kennedy; the SSA-based reformulation is **Cooper–Simpson–Vick OSR**, which finds induction variables as SCCs in the SSA graph headed by a loop φ and rewrites regions bottom-up). Modern compilers rest this on **Scalar Evolution (SCEV)**: closed-form **add-recurrence** expressions `{base, +, step}` per loop, composable (`{0,+,4}` = i*4), supporting trip-count computation (**backedge-taken count**), overflow reasoning via `nsw/nuw` flags, and **IV widening** (promote i32 IVs to i64 on 64-bit targets to kill sign-extensions). Named consumers: **IndVarSimplify** (canonicalize to a single canonical IV, replace exit conditions with computable exit values — **linear function test replacement (LFTR)**), **Loop Strength Reduce (LSR)** (a backend-oriented formulation choosing IV bases/scales to match target **addressing modes**, solving a cost minimization over candidate formulae with register-pressure terms), and trip-count-based **loop deletion** (loops with no side effects and computable exits removed entirely) and **induction-variable elimination**.

### 8.3 Loop Tiling (Blocking), Interchange, and the Unimodular/Polyhedral Framework

Locality transforms for loop nests. **Loop interchange** swaps nest levels to make the fastest-varying subscript match the innermost loop (stride-1 access, cache-line exploitation); legality requires the permuted **direction vectors** to remain lexicographically non-negative (no dependence becomes carried "backwards"). **Loop tiling (blocking)** strip-mines two or more dimensions and interchanges to iterate over B×B blocks, converting O(N) reuse distance into O(B) so working sets fit in L1/L2 (classic for matmul: i,j,k → it,jt,kt,i,j,k); legal when the band of loops is **fully permutable** (all dependence components non-negative in those dimensions), often enabled by **loop skewing** (change of basis i'=i, j'=j+f·i to make wavefront dependences tileable, e.g., stencils). The **unimodular transformation framework** (Wolf & Lam, Banerjee) treats interchange/skewing/reversal as unimodular integer matrices applied to the iteration space, legal iff every dependence vector maps to a lexicographically positive vector; the strictly more general **polyhedral model** represents statement instances as integer points in parametric polyhedra, dependences as affine relations, and transformations as per-statement **affine schedules**, with the **Pluto algorithm** (Bondhugula et al., PLDI 2008) finding schedules that minimize dependence distances (bounded by an affine cost function, solved with ILP/Farkas' lemma) to simultaneously enable tiling and coarse-grained parallelism; production incarnations include **Polly** (LLVM, over isl) and GCC's Graphite. Related nest transforms to name: **loop fusion** (merge adjacent loops over conformable iteration spaces to improve temporal locality / reduce overhead; legal if fusion introduces no fusion-preventing dependence reversal) and its inverse **loop distribution/fission** (split a loop to isolate a vectorizable or parallelizable portion, or to break a recurrence apart — used by LLVM's LoopDistribute to enable vectorization).

### 8.4 Unrolling-Family Transformations (brief)

**Loop unrolling** (full for constant small trip counts; partial by factor U with an epilogue or **runtime unrolling** with a prologue computing `n mod U`) reduces branch overhead and enlarges scheduling/SLP windows at i-cache cost; **unroll-and-jam** unrolls an outer loop and fuses the resulting inner-loop copies, increasing inner-loop ILP and register reuse for nests (legal when the outer loop carries no dependence that jamming would violate); **loop peeling** removes first iterations to resolve phase conditions (e.g., make a conditional invariant, align pointers, or enable LICM); **loop unswitching** hoists a loop-invariant conditional out of the loop by duplicating the loop under each branch (trading size for the elimination of in-loop control flow — LLVM's SimpleLoopUnswitch, including non-trivial unswitching of conditions feeding selects/guards); **loop idiom recognition** rewrites counted loops into `memset`/`memcpy`/popcount intrinsics; **loop rotation** converts while-loops into do-while (guarded) form, a canonicalization that makes LICM and latch-exit analysis effective.

## Cross-Cutting Observations

1. **Phase-ordering coupling is the real design problem.** Inlining manufactures the context that makes escape analysis, SROA, alias analysis, and vectorization succeed; SSA quality determines GVN/PRE power; scheduling and register allocation fight over the same resource (pre-RA scheduling must model pressure; allocators must not destroy schedules) — motivating integrated approaches (e.g., SSA-based RA, MISched's pressure-aware policy).
2. **Precision is bought with runtime checks.** Where static analysis fails — aliasing for vectorization, class hierarchies for inlining, escape paths for scalar replacement — production compilers insert guards (memchecks, class checks, materialization points) and pair them with fallback versions or deoptimization. This "optimistic + guard + recover" pattern recurs in every area above.
3. **Canonicalization enables everything.** LoopSimplify/LCSSA, pruned SSA, loop rotation, and IV canonicalization exist so that each heavyweight optimization can assume a normal form instead of handling arbitrary IR — a discipline as important as any individual algorithm.
